subjective.question: Write down the characteristics of enteropneusts.
subjective.answer: Enteropneusts (acorn worms, e.g. Balanoglossus) are marine hemichordates with the following characteristics: (1) The soft, worm-like body is divided into three regions — proboscis, collar and trunk. (2) The proboscis contains the stomochord, a hollow outgrowth of the buccal cavity once compared with the notochord. (3) The pharyngeal part of the trunk bears a series of paired gill slits opening to the exterior. (4) They live in U-shaped burrows in muddy or sandy sea shores and feed by ciliary-mucous feeding, trapping particles in mucus on the proboscis. (5) The coelom is divided into proboscis, collar and trunk cavities. (6) An excretory glomerulus is present on the proboscis. (7) Development includes a free-swimming tornaria larva resembling the larvae of echinoderms. (8) Sexes are separate and fertilisation is external.

subjective.question: Describe digestion in enteropneusts.
subjective.answer: Food, trapped in mucus on the proboscis and collar, is carried by cilia to the mouth and passes through the pharynx, where water escapes through the gill slits. From the pharynx the food cord enters the intestine. Digestion is extracellular and takes place in the intestine; the hepatic sacs (liver caeca), which are small outpocketings of the intestine, secrete digestive enzymes that act on the food. Nutrients are absorbed across the intestinal wall, and undigested material, together with ingested sand and mud, is passed out through the anus as castings. Enteropneusts are thus deposit and suspension feeders, and material may spend a long time passing through the gut while organic matter is extracted from it.

subjective.question: Explain osmoregulation in marine and freshwater fishes.
subjective.answer: Marine teleosts are hypo-osmotic to sea water, so they continually lose water and gain salts. They compensate by drinking sea water, excreting excess monovalent salts (Na+ and Cl-) through the chloride cells of the gills, and producing only a small volume of urine. Freshwater teleosts are hyper-osmotic to their medium, so water continually enters the body and salts are lost. They compensate by not drinking, by producing large volumes of very dilute urine to expel the excess water, and by actively absorbing salts through the gills (and from food) to replace those lost. Elasmobranchs take a different route: they retain urea so that their body fluids stay nearly iso-osmotic with sea water, and excrete excess salt through the rectal gland. Hagfishes are exceptional in being osmoconformers.

subjective.question: Give an explanation on Myxini (hagfishes).
subjective.answer: Myxini (hagfishes, e.g. Myxine) are jawless marine vertebrates (cyclostomes) with an elongated, eel-like body. They lack jaws, paired fins, scales and a vertebral column; the notochord persists throughout life as the axial support. The eyes are degenerate and buried under the skin. The mouth is surrounded by barbels and bears keratinous tooth plates on a tongue-like rasping organ used to tear flesh from dead or dying fishes on which they scavenge. Rows of slime glands along the body pour out enormous quantities of slime when the animal is disturbed, as a defence. They have a single terminal nostril, numerous gill openings, and are osmoconformers whose body fluids are nearly iso-osmotic with sea water — a condition unique among vertebrates. Sexes are separate and there is no larval stage.

subjective.question: Describe the partition of the atrium in caudates and anurans.
subjective.answer: The amphibian heart has two atria and a single ventricle. In anurans (frogs and toads) the division of the atrium is complete: an interatrial septum fully separates the right atrium, receiving oxygen-poor blood from the sinus venosus, from the left atrium, receiving oxygen-rich blood from the lungs, so mixing is reduced before blood enters the ventricle. In caudates (salamanders and newts) the partition is less complete: the interatrial septum is thin and perforated (fenestrated), so the separation of the two atrial streams is incomplete and more mixing of blood can occur. This difference reflects the greater reliance of many caudates on cutaneous and gill respiration and their generally lower metabolic demands compared with anurans.

subjective.question: In the context of vertebrates, what is the primary axial structure, and which class within the infraphylum possesses it? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: The primary axial structure is the notochord — a flexible, rod-like structure of vacuolated cells enclosed in a sheath, lying dorsal to the gut and ventral to the nerve cord. It is the first skeletal axis to appear in the embryo of every chordate. In most vertebrates it is largely replaced during development by the vertebral column. Within the infraphylum Vertebrata, it is retained as the functional axial skeleton throughout adult life in the jawless fishes — the class Myxini (hagfishes) (and largely in lampreys as well), which never develop a true vertebral column around it.

subjective.question: What are the eye adaptations of amphibians, and how do they respond to different light in eye vision? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: The amphibian eye is adapted for vision both in water and on land. Movable eyelids and a nictitating membrane protect the eye and keep the cornea moist on land. In air the cornea becomes the main refractive surface, while in water the nearly spherical lens does most of the focusing. Accommodation is achieved by moving the lens forward (towards the cornea) to focus on near objects, rather than by changing the lens shape. The retina contains both rods and cones; in dim light vision depends mainly on the rods and many amphibians are most active at dusk, while in bright light the cones and a contractile iris/pupil response protect the retina and allow colour and detail vision. Terrestrial forms also have well-developed tear (lacrimal) glands.

subjective.question: What is the role of the swim bladder in regulating buoyancy through gas secretion? (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The swim bladder is a gas-filled sac whose volume determines the fish's density and hence its buoyancy. In physoclistous fishes the bladder is closed, and gas is added by secretion and removed by absorption. Gas secretion takes place at the gas gland, supplied by the rete mirabile, a countercurrent bundle of capillaries. The gas gland releases lactic acid into the blood; the acid lowers the pH, and through the Root effect haemoglobin unloads oxygen even against a high oxygen pressure. The countercurrent arrangement of the rete multiplies this effect, so gas (mainly oxygen) diffuses into the bladder until its pressure balances the outside pressure, inflating the bladder and increasing buoyancy so the fish rises or holds its depth. When the fish needs to descend, gas is absorbed back into the blood at the oval body. By this secretion–absorption control the fish maintains neutral buoyancy at different depths without continuous swimming.

subjective.question: What are the challenges and conservation efforts related to turtle species? (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Challenges: (1) Loss and disturbance of nesting beaches through coastal development and artificial lighting, which disorients hatchlings. (2) Poaching of adults and collection of eggs for food and trade in shell and skin. (3) Accidental capture (bycatch) and drowning in trawl nets, gill nets and longlines. (4) Marine pollution — plastic bags are mistaken for jellyfish and eaten, and oil and debris degrade habitats. (5) Climate change: because sex is determined by nest temperature, warming produces strongly female-biased populations and floods nests. (6) Predation of eggs and hatchlings by animals increased near human settlements. Conservation efforts: legal protection of turtles and their nesting beaches (wildlife laws and CITES listing, which controls international trade), establishment of protected nesting reserves and hatcheries, mandatory use of Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs) in shrimp trawls, community patrols and eco-tourism that give local people an income from living turtles, public awareness programmes, and head-starting/release programmes for hatchlings.

subjective.question: Describe the feeding mechanism of Balanoglossus.
subjective.answer: Balanoglossus is a ciliary-mucous feeder. Glands of the proboscis secrete mucus, and particles from the burrow water and sediment stick to the mucus covering the proboscis and collar. Cilia beat so that the mucus sheet, loaded with food particles, is drawn back towards the mouth at the base of the proboscis. A special U-shaped ciliated groove (the pre-oral ciliary organ) tests the material, and rejected particles are diverted away, while the accepted mucus-food cord passes into the mouth and pharynx, where excess water leaves through the gill slits. The animal also swallows large quantities of sand and mud while burrowing and extracts the organic matter from it, voiding the residue as castings.

subjective.question: What is the stomochord? Discuss its homology.
subjective.answer: The stomochord is a hollow, forward outgrowth of the roof of the buccal cavity that projects into the proboscis of enteropneusts. It is made of tall vacuolated cells and supports the proboscis. Because of its position above the gut and its vacuolated cells, it was historically compared with the chordate notochord, and the group was named Hemichordata ('half chordates') on this basis. However, the stomochord is restricted to the proboscis, develops as a gut diverticulum rather than from chordamesoderm, and lacks the full organisation of a true notochord, so most zoologists now regard it as at most partly comparable with the notochord, and hemichordates are placed in their own phylum, closely related to echinoderms and chordates.

subjective.question: Write a note on the tornaria larva and its significance.
subjective.answer: The tornaria is the free-swimming, planktonic larva of enteropneusts such as Balanoglossus. It is small, oval and transparent, with ciliated bands (a pre-oral band and a circumferential telotroch) used in swimming and feeding, an apical tuft of cilia with eye spots, and a complete gut with mouth and anus. Its great significance is its close resemblance to the bipinnaria larva of starfishes: both share similar ciliated bands, coelomic pouches and an apical organ. This larval similarity is strong evidence that hemichordates and echinoderms share a common ancestor, and it supports placing Hemichordata near Echinodermata and Chordata in the deuterostome lineage. At metamorphosis the larva sinks, elongates and develops the proboscis, collar and trunk of the adult.

subjective.question: Describe the body divisions and coelom of Balanoglossus.
subjective.answer: The body is divided into three regions. (1) The proboscis (protosome) is a muscular, conical anterior part used in burrowing; it contains a single proboscis coelom, the stomochord and the excretory glomerulus. (2) The collar (mesosome) is a short muscular ring behind the proboscis, containing a pair of collar coeloms, and it bears the mouth on its ventral side. (3) The trunk (metasome) is the long posterior region containing paired trunk coeloms; its anterior part bears the gill slits and hepatic sacs, and it houses the intestine and gonads. The coelomic cavities of the proboscis and collar open to the exterior by small pores and can be filled with water, helping the animal burrow by hydraulic action.

subjective.question: Compare hagfishes and lampreys.
subjective.answer: Both are jawless cyclostomes with eel-like bodies, no paired fins and a persistent notochord, but they differ in several ways. Hagfishes (Myxini) are strictly marine scavengers with degenerate eyes, a single nostril, keratinous tooth plates, numerous slime glands, and body fluids iso-osmotic with sea water; they lack a larval stage. Lampreys (Petromyzontida) live in both marine and fresh water, have well-developed eyes, a sucker-like oral disc with horny teeth used to attach to fishes and feed on blood and flesh, seven pairs of gill pouches, and a distinct filter-feeding larva (ammocoete) that lives buried in river sediment for several years before metamorphosis. Hagfishes also lack any trace of vertebrae, whereas lampreys possess rudimentary cartilaginous vertebral elements (arcualia).

subjective.question: Write a note on the slime glands of hagfishes.
subjective.answer: Hagfishes possess rows of large slime glands along each side of the body. Each gland contains thread cells and mucous cells. When a hagfish is seized or threatened, the glands discharge their contents through pores; on contact with sea water the secretion expands almost instantly into a large volume of extremely slippery slime. The slime clogs the gills and mouth of predators, forcing them to release the hagfish, and it also lubricates the body so the animal can slip out of a predator's grip or tie itself in a knot to gain leverage while tearing food. The hagfish cleans itself by passing a body knot along its length to strip off the slime.

subjective.question: Differentiate between physostomous and physoclistous swim bladders.
subjective.answer: In the physostomous condition, found in many primitive teleosts (e.g. carps and eels), the swim bladder remains connected to the gut by an open pneumatic duct, and the fish can fill or empty the bladder by gulping or releasing air at the surface. In the physoclistous condition, found in most advanced teleosts, the pneumatic duct is lost in the adult and the bladder is a closed sac: gas is added internally by the gas gland and rete mirabile (secretion) and removed through the vascular oval body (absorption). The physoclistous arrangement frees the fish from needing access to the surface and allows precise buoyancy control at depth.

subjective.question: Explain the role of the rete mirabile and the Root effect in swim-bladder filling.
subjective.answer: The rete mirabile is a bundle of many parallel arterial and venous capillaries supplying the gas gland, arranged so that blood flows in opposite directions in adjacent vessels (countercurrent). The gas gland secretes lactic acid into the blood. The lowered pH acts on haemoglobin through the Root effect, forcing it to release oxygen even when the surrounding oxygen pressure is already high. Because of the countercurrent arrangement, the acid and released gas are retained and progressively concentrated along the rete (countercurrent multiplication), building up a very high gas pressure that drives oxygen (and other gases) into the bladder lumen. In deep-sea fishes this mechanism can generate pressures of many atmospheres inside the bladder.

subjective.question: How does a freshwater fish maintain its water and salt balance?
subjective.answer: A freshwater teleost is hyper-osmotic to its surroundings, so water floods in osmotically across the gills and body surface while salts tend to leak out and are lost in urine. The fish maintains balance by: (1) not drinking water; (2) producing a very large volume of extremely dilute urine through well-developed glomerular kidneys, expelling the excess water while reabsorbing most salts in the kidney tubules; (3) actively taking up Na+ and Cl- from the water through ion-transporting (chloride) cells in the gills, against the concentration gradient; and (4) obtaining additional salts from food. Together these keep the blood concentration steady at about one-third that of sea water.

subjective.question: How do elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) solve the osmotic problem of living in the sea?
subjective.answer: Sharks and rays retain large amounts of urea (and the stabilising compound trimethylamine oxide, TMAO) in their blood and tissues. This raises the internal osmotic concentration to slightly above that of sea water, so instead of losing water they gain a small amount osmotically and do not need to drink. Excess water is removed by the kidneys as urine. Salts that enter with food or diffuse in are excreted by a special rectal gland, which secretes a concentrated NaCl solution, while the gills are relatively impermeable to urea. This ureosmotic strategy is energetically different from the teleost strategy of drinking sea water and pumping salt out at the gills.

subjective.question: Describe the heart of an amphibian and how blood flows through it.
subjective.answer: The amphibian heart has a sinus venosus, two atria (right and left, divided by an interatrial septum — complete in anurans, perforated in caudates) and a single ventricle leading into a conus/truncus arteriosus. Oxygen-poor blood from the body enters the right atrium via the sinus venosus, while oxygen-rich blood from the lungs enters the left atrium. Both atria discharge into the single ventricle, where the spongy inner wall (trabeculae) and the timing of contraction limit mixing. A spiral valve in the conus arteriosus helps direct oxygen-poor blood mainly into the pulmocutaneous arches (to lungs and skin) and oxygen-rich blood into the systemic and carotid arches (to body and head). Separation is therefore partial but functionally effective.

subjective.question: Discuss the adaptations of amphibians for terrestrial life.
subjective.answer: Amphibians show several adaptations to land, though they remain tied to water. (1) Pentadactyl limbs with girdles support the body and allow walking. (2) Lungs replace gills as the main respiratory organs in adults, supplemented by cutaneous respiration through moist, glandular skin. (3) The heart's double circulation (separate pulmonary circuit) improves oxygen delivery. (4) Eyelids, a nictitating membrane and lacrimal glands protect and moisten the eye, and the cornea becomes the main refractive surface in air. (5) A middle-ear cavity with a tympanum and columella transmits airborne sound. (6) The skin contains mucous glands to reduce drying and poison glands for defence. However, their eggs lack a shell and must be laid in water or moist places, and the larva is aquatic, so reproduction still depends on water.

subjective.question: Describe the shell of a turtle and its functions.
subjective.answer: The turtle shell is a bony box formed from expanded ribs and vertebrae fused with dermal bones, covered externally by keratinous scutes. The domed dorsal part is the carapace and the flatter ventral part is the plastron; the two are joined at the sides by bony bridges. The shell functions primarily as armour: the head, limbs and tail can be withdrawn into it in many land and freshwater forms, protecting the animal from predators. It also provides support and attachment for muscles and protects the internal organs. Its disadvantages are weight and rigidity — the ribs cannot move for breathing, so turtles ventilate their lungs by movements of limb and throat muscles, and the shell limits flexibility and speed.

subjective.question: What is temperature-dependent sex determination in turtles, and why is it a conservation concern?
subjective.answer: In most turtles, the sex of the offspring is not fixed by chromosomes but by the temperature of the nest during the middle part of incubation: in sea turtles, cooler temperatures produce mainly males and warmer temperatures mainly females. This is a conservation concern because global warming is raising sand temperatures, producing strongly female-biased hatchling sex ratios and, at extreme temperatures, reducing hatching success. A population with too few males may eventually fail to reproduce effectively. Conservation responses include shading or relocating nests to cooler sites, protecting a range of nesting beaches with different temperature profiles, and monitoring sex ratios as an indicator of climate impact.
